Explain in your own words what 'Anther and Microsporangium Wall Layers' refers to.
questions.a: A stamen carries a slender filament topped by an anther that is typically two-lobed and four-sporangiate; every microsporangium is jacketed by epidermis, endothecium, middle layers and an innermost tapetum.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Anther and Microsporangium Wall Layers'.
questions.a: The tapetum feeds the growing pollen, while the outer three jackets shield the sporangium and help it split open at maturity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Anther and Microsporangium Wall Layers' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2.1 (source: lebo101.txt lines 116-157 (stamen, anther section and microsporangium structure))

concepts.title: Pollen Wall, Shedding Stage and Viability

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Pollen Wall, Shedding Stage and Viability' refers to.
questions.a: A pollen grain wears a chemically tough sporopollenin exine broken by germ pores over a thin cellulose-pectin intine, and it leaves the anther either two-celled or three-celled, remaining viable from half an hour in cereals to months in some other families.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pollen Wall, Shedding Stage and Viability'.
questions.a: Sporopollenin resists heat, acids, alkalis and every known enzyme, which is why pollen survives as fossils, while germ pores mark the spots where the pollen tube later emerges.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Pollen Wall, Shedding Stage and Viability' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2.1 (source: lebo101.txt lines 179-247 (pollen grain structure, 2-celled/3-celled stages, viability and storage))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Ovule (Megasporangium) Structure' refers to.
questions.a: An ovule grows on the placenta through a stalk called the funicle, joins it at the hilum, and wraps a reserve-filled nucellus in one or two integuments that leave a micropylar opening, with the chalaza forming the base opposite the micropyle.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Ovule (Megasporangium) Structure'.
questions.a: A single embryo sac, the female gametophyte, sits embedded in the nucellus of a typical ovule.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Ovule (Megasporangium) Structure' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2.2 (source: lebo101.txt lines 248-285 (pistil parts and megasporangium structure))

concepts.title: Megasporogenesis, Monosporic Development and Embryo Sac Organisation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Megasporogenesis, Monosporic Development and Embryo Sac Organisation' refers to.
questions.a: A large, densely cytoplasmic megaspore mother cell in the micropylar nucellus divides meiotically into four haploid megaspores; three degenerate and the lone survivor, through repeated free-nuclear mitoses and later wall formation, builds an eight-nucleate, seven-celled embryo sac.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Megasporogenesis, Monosporic Development and Embryo Sac Organisation'.
questions.a: Monosporic development means a single functional megaspore constructs the whole female gametophyte, ending with egg apparatus, antipodals and a two-polar-nucleus central cell.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Megasporogenesis, Monosporic Development and Embryo Sac Organisation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2.2 (source: lebo101.txt lines 286-347 (megasporogenesis and female gametophyte development))

concepts.title: Kinds of Pollination: Autogamy, Geitonogamy and Xenogamy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Kinds of Pollination: Autogamy, Geitonogamy and Xenogamy' refers to.
questions.a: Pollen movement is classified by source: autogamy lands pollen on the stigma of the same flower, geitonogamy moves it to another flower of the same plant, and xenogamy carries it between different plants, only the last delivering genetically unlike pollen.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Kinds of Pollination: Autogamy, Geitonogamy and Xenogamy'.
questions.a: Closed cleistogamous flowers force self-pollination and assure seed set, whereas xenogamy alone counts as true genetic cross-pollination.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Kinds of Pollination: Autogamy, Geitonogamy and Xenogamy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2.3 (source: lebo101.txt lines 348-421 (kinds of pollination))

concepts.title: Agents of Pollination and Floral Adaptations

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Agents of Pollination and Floral Adaptations' refers to.
questions.a: Wind, water and animals carry pollen between flowers, and each agent stamps a signature set of floral traits: light non-sticky pollen with feathery stigmas for wind, mucilage-coated ribbon pollen for water, and colour, scent plus nectar rewards for animal visitors.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Agents of Pollination and Floral Adaptations'.
questions.a: Biotic agents, especially bees, dominate pollination, and flowers pay for the service with nectar, pollen or egg-laying sites.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Agents of Pollination and Floral Adaptations' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2.3 (source: lebo101.txt lines 422-564 (agents of pollination, wind water and animal examples))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Outbreeding Devices and Self-Incompatibility' refers to.
questions.a: Flowering plants curb inbreeding depression by desynchronising pollen release from stigma receptivity, placing anthers and stigma far apart, blocking self pollen genetically through self-incompatibility, or producing unisexual flowers on the same or separate plants.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Outbreeding Devices and Self-Incompatibility'.
questions.a: Monoecy such as castor or maize still allows geitonogamy, but dioecy like papaya shuts out both autogamy and geitonogamy.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Outbreeding Devices and Self-Incompatibility' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2.3 (source: lebo101.txt lines 565-584 (outbreeding devices))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Pollen-Pistil Interaction and Artificial Hybridisation' refers to.
questions.a: The pistil chemically interrogates every landed grain, fostering germination and tube growth of compatible pollen while rejecting wrong or self pollen, and breeders exploit this gatekeeping by emasculating flower buds and bagging them so only chosen pollen reaches the stigma.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pollen-Pistil Interaction and Artificial Hybridisation'.
questions.a: Emasculation followed by bagging, dusting with desired pollen and rebagging guarantees a controlled cross, and unisexual female parents need no emasculation at all.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Pollen-Pistil Interaction and Artificial Hybridisation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2.3 (source: lebo101.txt lines 585-665 (pollen-pistil interaction and hybridisation techniques))

concepts.title: Double Fertilisation: Syngamy and Triple Fusion

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Double Fertilisation: Syngamy and Triple Fusion' refers to.
questions.a: After the pollen tube empties into a synergid, one sperm unites with the egg to make a diploid zygote while the other unites with the two polar nuclei of the central cell to make a triploid primary endosperm nucleus, two fusions occurring together in a single embryo sac.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Double Fertilisation: Syngamy and Triple Fusion'.
questions.a: Double fertilisation pairs syngamy with triple fusion and is exclusive to flowering plants, setting up embryo and endosperm side by side.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Double Fertilisation: Syngamy and Triple Fusion' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: lebo101.txt lines 681-693 (double fertilisation section))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Endosperm, Embryo and Seed Development' refers to.
questions.a: The primary endosperm cell multiplies ahead of the embryo, first as a free-nuclear tissue like coconut water and later cellular; the waiting zygote then passes through proembryo, globular and heart-shaped stages, and the finished ovule ripens into a seed inside a fruit whose wall derives from the ovary.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Endosperm, Embryo and Seed Development'.
questions.a: Dicot embryos carry two cotyledons on an axis with epicotyl and hypocotyl, while grass embryos replace one cotyledon by a scutellum and sheathe their shoot and root tips in coleoptile and coleorrhiza.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Endosperm, Embryo and Seed Development' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.4 (source: lebo101.txt lines 670-789 (endosperm, embryo, seed and fruit sections))

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Apomixis and Polyembryony' refers to.
questions.a: Apomixis builds seeds with no fertilisation at all, either from an unreduced diploid egg or from nucellar cells, and when several embryos share one seed, as in Citrus and mango, the condition is polyembryony.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Apomixis and Polyembryony'.
questions.a: Locking apomixis into hybrid crops would let farmers resow their own seed every season without the progeny losing hybrid character.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Apomixis and Polyembryony' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.5 (source: lebo101.txt lines 851-909 (apomixis, polyembryony and hybrid seed significance))
